newsitem.title: USA: Meeting plans seen soon in Conrail battle.
newsitem.headline: Meeting plans seen soon in Conrail battle.

text.p: Both sides in the takeover battle for Conrail Inc. said Thursday arrangements would be made soon for a meeting on resolving the impasse, but analysts and traders said it was uncertain a deal could struck.

"Based on their public comments, both sides are going into potential settlement talks with the expectation that each will come out the winner. This makes a near-term settlement somewhat less likely," said Prudential Securities analyst Brian Routledge.
"Both sides seem to be saying that their merger proposal must be the starting point," he said.

The chairmen of Conrail and CSX Corp., who have agreed on a cash and stock merger now worth $9.6 billion, told rival Conrail bidder Norfolk Southern Corp. in a letter on Wednesday they would be willing to meet for "meaningful and candid" discussions on the deal.

This was in response to a letter from Norfolk Southern Chairman David Goode offering talks, on the condition that its promise to deliver $115 per share to Conrail shareholders be recognized. Norfolk Southern's all-cash, $115 per-share bid is worth $10.3 billion.
Norfolk Southern spokesman Bob Fort said Thursday that the condition would not bar a meeting, and he expected a date to be set soon.
"They haven't started hammering out details for a meeting time," Fort said. "I'm sure that there's not going to be a long delay before that starts to happen."
Conrail spokesman Rudy Husband said expectations of a meeting soon were "a fair characterization."
CSX Chairman John Snow said at an earnings presentation Thursday, "I have high hopes the talks will lead to some mutually advantageous resolution of the things that divide us."
He reiterated that CSX was "committed to the merger with Conrail," but said CSX was prepared to make "meaningful concessions" to complete the deal.

"We have in mind granting Norfolk Southern access whether by ownership or trackage, etc... to give them a competitive system while sustaining as many of the benefits as possible," from the proposed Conrail merger, Snow said.

Analysts and traders said it was difficult to imagine how the Norfolk Southern and CSX-Conrail positions could be recognized. "Both sides are saying 'I want to buy it, and I'll give you what I don't want,'" said a takeover stock trader.
He said the talks may be meant to appease federal regulators whose approval is necessary for any deal and who have urged the three parties to discuss their differences.

Separately, Conrail and Norfolk Southern reported official results of a Conrail shareholder vote Friday which rejected a key company charter change that would have allowed the CSX-Conrail merger to proceed.
The results revealed that 49.9 million shares, or 65 percent of those voted, were against the proposal, and 26.8 million, or 35 percent supported it.
About 29 percent of shares held in a Conrail employee stock option program were against the proposal, Norfolk Southern said.

Conrail Chairman David LeVan, in a statement, attributed the defeat to an offer by Norfolk Southern to buy 9.9 percent of Conrail shares for $115 each as soon as the CSX merger was blocked. Norfolk Southern launched its tender offer for the stakeon Wednesday.
LeVan said, "The Conrail board of directors remains fully committed to the CSX-Conrail merger and will not approve a transaction with Norfolk Southern."

The margin of defeat was greater than initially estimated by Norfolk Southern. "We certainly hope Conrail's board will act in accordance with the wishes of Conrail shareholders," Norfolk Southern said in a statement.
Also on Thursday, CSX reported net income of $855 million for 1996, against $618 million, after a restructuring charge of $160 million, for 1995.
Fourth-quarter net income for 1996 was $253 million, against $276 million in 1995, a figure which included a $51 million one-time gain.
In addition, Conrail said it had reassigned two senior executives to focus on the merger.
